# Jupiter routing (Solana)

ACEX uses Jupiter v6 for CapShare ↔ USDC swaps on Solana instead of an on-chain AMM (EVM uses `PulseAMM`).

## Client

Python helper: `integrations/jupiter.py`
    
    from acex.integrations.jupiter import fetch_jupiter_quote, build_swap_plan
    
    quote = await fetch_jupiter_quote(
        input_mint=cap_share_mint,
        output_mint=usdc_mint,
        amount=1_000_000,  # base units
        slippage_bps=50,
    )
    plan = build_swap_plan(quote, user_public_key="...")

## Environment

Variable  | Default
--- | ---
`ACEX_JUPITER_QUOTE_URL`  | `https://quote-api.jup.ag/v6/quote`
`ACEX_JUPITER_SWAP_URL`  | `https://quote-api.jup.ag/v6/swap`
`ACEX_SOLANA_USDC_MINT`  | mainnet USDC

## Pulse Terminal flow

  1. `GET /api/v2/capital/pricing?chain=solana` — index + share reference prices
  2. Jupiter quote for execution size
  3. Wallet signs swap tx from Jupiter `/swap` response

See Pulse Terminal.

# Why does my uncensored AI still refuse?

Uncensoring reduces refusals but rarely removes them all: Heretic's own Gemma test still refused 3 of 100 prompts. Host filters, terms of service and mainstream models do the rest.

By ModelRanker · 2026-10-21

An “uncensored” model can still refuse for several reasons, and only some of them are about the model. Abliteration removes the main refusal direction, not every trace of refusal: Heretic’s own test on Gemma-3-12B still left 3 refusals out of 100. On top of that, the service may add its own filter or system prompt, its terms may rule out whole categories (NoTrack calls itself “99.9% uncensored” and lists 10 restricted items), or the model you’re talking to may not be uncensored at all.

## 1. Uncensoring reduces refusals, it doesn’t delete them

The research behind abliteration found that a single direction in a model’s activations carries most of the refusal signal. Most, not all. Removing it makes a model far more willing, but some refusals and hedges can survive, especially with older or cruder recipes. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A REFUSAL is an act of speech that belongs to the so-called critical speech acts. Its implementation poses a threat to the interaction balance between the sender and the recipient. For this reason, language uses resort to a variety of verbal and non-verbal strategies related to REFUSAL. A special case of the implementation of this speech act are letters of rejection for job applications, in which the refusal should – directly or indirectly – be expressed. Senders of this genre of texts formulate the refusal in different ways. This article examines the forms in which the speech act REFUSAL is implemented in German, drawing from the aforementioned genre. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I aim to show how thinking about gestures as such may lead us to an alternative politics of refusal. Recent scholarship in human geography has engaged ‘refusal’ as a concept for understanding how marginalised subjects and communities set limits on participation in, and incorporation by, dominant political and epistemic frameworks. This engagement draws on foundational interventions by Simpson (2007, 2014, 2017) and TallBear (2013), whose work on Indigenous sovereignty theorises refusal as a practice of withholding recognition and delimiting the terms of engagement with settler states, and by Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang, who frame refusal as a stance against extractive research logics (2014). Carole McGranahan further consolidates this approach by emphasising how refusal is generative rather than simply oppositional (2016). Human geographers have extended these insights into analyses of borders, migration and colonial power, as well as into methodological debates about fieldwork and the ethics of access, where refusal is understood as enacted through withholding, non-participation and limits on knowledge production (Guasco 2022; Jones 2012; Meier 2023; Wright 2018). Notably, for the emergence of negative geographies, Dekeyser and Jellis turn to refusal as a means of ‘staying with the tension’ and not simply reversing affirmationism to find a space for negative geographies (2021).

At the same time, there remains some ambiguity regarding the degree to which refusal may be understood as a conscious and strategic decision. Accounts grounded in Indigenous politics often emphasise refusal as an intentional act: a deliberate withholding, disengagement or non-compliance that asserts sovereignty and sets limits on recognition. Recent work in human geography suggests a different but complementary approach. Analyses of encounters within politically constrained environments indicate that what is interpreted as refusal can emerge through situated, relational and sometimes tacit practices. Jones (2012) follows the unauthorised border-crossing into India by a 62-year-old woman from Bangladesh, where she works as a servant for a wealthy family, to spend a month visiting her son and grandson. Jones's concept of ‘spaces of refusal’ shows how everyday practices of evasion and disregard can refuse to abide by the state's binary territorial and identity categories, even when they do not take the form of overt political resistance. Accordingly, refusal may involve partial disengagement, strategic ambiguity or forms of non-participation that are not always framed by participants themselves as deliberate acts. From this perspective, refusal may be better understood as a situated practice that is not reducible to conscious, intentional decision-making, including more ambiguous forms of disengagement under conditions of constraint. Following this thread of ambiguity, recent studies attending to gestures in human geography are concerned with how gestures articulate a certain politics of refusal by Black queer women in American gentrifying neighbourhoods (Adeyemi 2019; Seitz and Proudfoot 2021), by Palestinian people expressing humour and laughter in the heavily surveilled environment of border control security (Bhungalia 2020), and by people in Delhi taking over unfinished urban development projects ‘through practices of squatting and repair’ (Boudreau 2023; Simone et al. 2023).

This paper contributes to this thread of scholarship tracing the ambiguity of refusal through a theorisation of gestures as the medium through which the body goes on strike—unlike a conventional labour strike because it operates without intentionality—or, in other words, its inoperative refusal. To find one of the most sustained engagements with gestures and the connection between the psyche and the body, I will now turn to psychoanalysis and the writing of Winnicott. It is in this literature that I will argue for a reclaiming of the unconscious for the body via gestures.

# The Clearing

JJJJJerome Ellis

4.57 14 ratings 2 reviews

JJJJJerome Ellis’s The Clearing asks how stuttering, blackness, and music can be practices of refusal against hegemonic governance of time, speech, and encounter. Taking his glottal block stutter as a point of departure, Ellis figures the aporia and the block as clearing to consider how dysfluency, opacity, and refusal can open a new space for relation. Stemming from Ellis's essay "The Music, dysfluency, Blackness, and time,” published in 2020 in the Journal of Interdisciplinary Voice Studies (Volume 5, Issue 2) the present volume transcribes and translates his investigation across genres and media, turning to the page to How can a book bear the trace of music, and the racialized, disabled body?
